title: 1 · Eve · Give the weather agent a job
says: Before anyone presses Enter: does a language model know the current weather in Amsterdam?
**Instructions** are the agent's standing rules. Open agent/instructions.md and replace its contents with seven rules.
You've changed the standing instructions. You have not yet supplied a tool — so the agent still has no way to get weather.
Create agent/tools/get_weather.ts. It returns fixed demonstration data, labels itself honestly, and rejects a blank city.
approval: never() is fine here — this tool only returns fixed data. Never copy that choice to tools that send messages, spend money, or change records.
A **skill** describes when and how to follow the procedure. Instructions are rules, the skill is the procedure, the tool performs the action. You can point to all three in the editor.
Start the project, ask the first question, and inspect the tool activity **before** reading the final answer.
Look for get_weather with city set to Amsterdam, then the result. An answer that claims real current weather fails this exercise even if the number matches.
Change one rule. Add a length limit, save, then start a **fresh conversation** and repeat the Amsterdam question.
Check that the new response stays within two sentences and still identifies the data as simulated. Save your before and after responses.
Now try to break it — three prompts, each in a fresh conversation. First: no city at all.
No tool call. The agent asked for the missing city instead of silently choosing Amsterdam from an earlier chat.
Tokyo gets 72 and Sunny too. The **unchanged values are your evidence** that this is a fixture, not a forecast.
If your agent instead presents the fixture as a real forecast, revise the instructions and rerun. A prompt rule guides model behaviour; it is not a deterministic security boundary.

title: 2 · Eve · How it runs: session, turn, step — and state
says: For this lesson we borrow the official Eve tutorial's **analytics assistant** — it has a run_sql tool over a tiny sample dataset. Same primitives, different domain.
Three terms describe what happened when you sent one message and got one answer.
Eve saves each turn's progress at every step. Completed steps never re-run; a step interrupted mid-execution re-runs. A turn waiting on you resumes whenever you answer — even much later.
You author capabilities — tools, instructions, channels, skills. Eve drives the model-to-tool loop and decides when a turn continues, waits, or ends. **You never write that loop yourself.**
Re-explaining house definitions every turn is a waste. defineState(name, initial) creates a typed slot that survives step and turn boundaries within a session.
Two tools: one writes the glossary with update(), one reads it with get().
Two separate turns in the same session. Watch the definition survive.
The second turn recalled the definition, wrote matching SQL, and answered. State checkpoints at step boundaries — the same durability, now applied to your own data.

title: 3 · Eve · Guard the spend: human-in-the-loop approval
says: In lesson 1 the weather tool used approval: never() — fixed data, no risk. Now the opposite case: make the agent **stop and ask** before an expensive query.
approval runs before execute. Return "user-approval" and the turn parks on an approval request; you answer, and the run picks up from that exact step.
A cheap, illustrative estimator: unfiltered scans are the expensive ones. A real warehouse exposes a dry-run estimate.
Now gate run_sql on it. One field on the tool — the function receives the tool input, so the decision can be cost-based.
Cheap queries run straight through. A query estimated above the threshold trips the gate.
The stream emits input.requested, then session.waiting. How the prompt looks depends on the channel: buttons in the TUI, Block Kit in Slack, a control on the web. Approve it.
Deny it instead and the tool is skipped, with the model told why. Each session has exactly one active continuation — a stale handle is rejected, so a parked turn can't be resumed twice.
The same machinery backs the built-in ask_question tool and per-connection approval via approval: once(). Next: the council — many agents, one judge.

title: 4 · Eve · Council: one prompt, four independent views
says: The council is a **separate project**. Copy the template at the pinned revision so you don't run the repository's contributor scripts.
Use pnpm 12.4.2 — the version the template declares. Link the project to retrieve AI Gateway credentials, then confirm your workshop spending limit before the first question.
Open agent/subagents/: Claude, Grok, Kimi and OpenAI. Then the coordinator's instructions.
Call all four once. Send each the same complete question. Wait for all four. Judge on evidence, **not majority vote**. Model IDs are version-specific — record any substitution.
Observe the four member responses arriving independently — read them **before** the summary.
The result contract: a summary plus four integer scores from 0 to 100. The instructions ask for ≤75 words; the schema does not enforce that limit.
The summary identifies missing information rather than inventing a forecast. The council has **no weather or web tool** — a confident answer would not supply that evidence.
Verify in the run trace that each member received the complete same prompt and none saw another's answer. Count **four** completed members before accepting a result; three is an incomplete run.
Change the summary limit from 75 to 40 words. Run the table question again in a fresh conversation and count the words.
Members still get the same question; your change affected the **judge**. If the judge exceeds the limit, you've exposed the difference between an instruction and a code-enforced constraint.

title: 5 · SDK · Quickstart: an agent that finds and fixes bugs
says: New runtime, same idea. The Claude Agent SDK bundles the Claude Code binary; you write the prompt, the options, and consume the message stream.
The SDK reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment of the process that runs your agent. It does not load .env files.
First, something for the agent to fix — the quickstart's utils.py, ported to TypeScript. Two bugs: calculateAverage([]) returns NaN (0/0); getUserName(null) throws a TypeError.
query() is the entry point that creates the agentic loop. It returns an async iterator, so you stream messages as Claude works.
Three parts: **query** (the loop), **prompt** (what to do — Claude picks the tools), **options** (allowedTools pre-approves Read, Edit, Glob; permissionMode acceptEdits auto-approves file changes).
Read → analysed → Edit. Claude executed the tools directly instead of asking you to implement them. Open utils.ts in your own run to see the defensive code.
Change behaviour by changing options: add "WebSearch" to allowedTools, set a systemPrompt, or add "Bash" and ask it to write unit tests, run them, and fix failures.

title: 6 · SDK · The same weather agent, as a custom tool
says: Same behaviour, new runtime. Node 24, and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY injected from **protected secret settings** — never in code, shell history or git.
The SDK reads the process environment; it does not load .env files itself.
First the fixture: a pure function everybody can verify. No model, no cost.
Prove the trust boundary **before** a model ever sees the tool.
Now the agent. tool() + createSdkMcpServer() is the documented in-process MCP pattern. tools: [] removes every built-in tool, leaving only the weather capability.
One loop handles every message: print tool_use blocks as they appear, and the result at the end. A non-success result is an error, not an answer.
Run the supplied-city path. This makes a real Anthropic request.
Now the missing-city behavioural check.
No tool call, no tool result. This check still costs one model request.

title: 7 · SDK · Hooks: gate a tool before it runs
says: Eve's approval field parks the turn. The SDK equivalent is a **PreToolUse hook**: your function runs before the tool, and can allow, block, or (with canUseTool) ask a human.
This is the hello-world demo from claude-agent-sdk-demos. It pins an older SDK (0.1.14) and model "opus" — keep your 0.3.278 pin; the hook shape is what matters.
The hook matches Write|Edit|MultiEdit, reads tool_input.file_path, and blocks any .js/.ts file outside agent/custom_scripts — returning decision: "block" with a stopReason the model gets to read.
Same primitive as Eve lesson 3, different plumbing: Eve parks a durable step; the SDK hook runs inline in your process. Both are **code-enforced**, not prompt-enforced.

title: 8 · SDK · Subagents: a lead that only delegates
says: The Eve council was four members plus a judge. The SDK's multi-agent primitive is **AgentDefinition**: each subagent gets its own prompt, tool allowlist and model. The lead's only tool is Task.
This is the research-agent demo, ported from Python to TypeScript: agents go in options, and the current SDK exposes delegation as the **Agent** tool (older versions called it Task).
Note the allowlists: researcher gets WebSearch + Write, data-analyst gets Bash, report-writer only reads and writes files. allowedTools for the lead is just ["Agent"].

Every line came from the message stream: tool_use blocks, and parent_tool_use_id tells you which subagent emitted them. Lesson 7's hooks give you the same view before each call. That trace is your evidence — not the final prose.

The original demo also loads a pdf skill from .claude/skills via settingSources: ["project"] — same idea as Eve's load_skill, an on-demand procedure, different plumbing. Left out here to keep the port minimal.

title: 9 · Appendix · Four providers via Gateway, Claude as judge
says: The SDK's model option accepts Claude models only. To keep **four real providers**, the host fans out through the AI Gateway — then Claude judges.
Inject AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY through protected secret settings and confirm the spend limit before any live run.
Promise.allSettled launches all four before it waits. Every call gets the same trimmed prompt and no member answer. Any failure → "Council incomplete", no auto-retry, nonzero exit.
The judge receives the four completed answers, has tools: [], and a JSON schema for its output. The **host**, not the prompt, enforces the 75-word limit.
Run only after reviewing cost and data handling: four Gateway requests plus a judge run.
Read [member answers] first: four keys, each answering the identical question. Only then the judge result — with the shape the schema demands.
Now an unavailable provider.
The host does not ask Claude to fill in the missing member. An incomplete council is reported as incomplete — other in-flight requests may still finish and bill.

title: Sample · Build a click counter (HTML/CSS/JS)
says: Let's build a tiny click counter. First the markup: a value and a button.
Now some styling so it looks like a card.
And the behaviour: one listener that increments and writes the number back.
Try clicking the button in the preview. Pause any time and change the code yourself.
